competition: Polish Junior Mathematical Olympiad (Olimpiada Matematyczna Juniorów), Final Round

problems.problem: How many quadruples $(a,b,c,d)$ of positive integers satisfy the equation $ab+bc+cd+da=55$? Justify your answer.

A parallelogram $ABCD$ is given. Point $E$ lies on side $AB$, and point $F$ on side $AD$. Line $EF$ meets line $CB$ at point $P$ and line $CD$ at point $Q$. Prove that the area of triangle $CEF$ is equal to the area of triangle $APQ$.

In space, $n$ points are given ($n \geqslant 4$) such that no four of them lie in one plane. Every two of these points are joined by a blue or a red segment. Prove that one of these colours can be chosen so that every two points are joined by a segment or a broken line of the chosen colour.

A tetrahedron is given such that every dihedral angle determined by two of its adjacent faces is acute or right. The vertices of this tetrahedron lie on a sphere with centre $S$. Can the point $S$ lie outside this polyhedron? Justify your answer.

Distinct primes $p$, $q$ and positive integers $a$, $b$ are given such that the number $aq$ leaves remainder $1$ when divided by $p$, and the number $bp$ leaves remainder $1$ when divided by $q$. Prove that $$\frac{a}{p}+\frac{b}{q}>1.$$
Determine all triples $(a,b,c)$ of real numbers satisfying the system of equations $$\begin{cases} ab=a+b\\ bc=b+c\\ ca=c+a \end{cases}$$

Each vertex of a regular 100-gon is to be assigned a positive real number. Is there such an assignment in which every number is equal to the absolute value of the difference of the numbers adjacent to it? Justify your answer.

In an acute triangle $ABC$, points $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of sides $AC$ and $BC$, respectively. The altitude of triangle $ABC$ drawn from vertex $C$ meets segment $MN$ at point $D$. The perpendicular bisector of side $AB$ meets segment $MN$ at point $E$. Prove that $MD=NE$.
How many numbers $n$ in the set $\{1,2,\ldots,2007\}$ are there for which the number $n^4-1$ is divisible by $9$? Justify your answer.
Is there a quadrilateral pyramid each of whose lateral faces is a right triangle? Justify your answer.

Real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ are given such that the numbers $$ab+bc,\quad bc+ca,\quad ca+ab$$ are positive. Prove that the numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ have the same sign, i.e. either all of them are positive or all of them are negative.
Prove that there exist infinitely many triples $(a,b,c)$ of positive integers satisfying the equality $$a^3+3b^6=c^2.$$

A triangle $ABC$ is given in which $AC>BC$. Point $P$ is the orthogonal projection of point $B$ onto the bisector of angle $ACB$. Point $M$ is the midpoint of segment $AB$. Given that $$BC=a,\quad CA=b,\quad AB=c,$$ compute the length of segment $PM$.

Can the vertices of a regular 20-gon be numbered with the numbers $1,2,\ldots,20$ so that all of these numbers are used and, for every four consecutive vertices, the sum of their numbers is less than $43$? Justify your answer.

A regular quadrilateral pyramid is given, each of whose edges has length $1$. The pyramid was cut by a plane intersecting all of its lateral edges, and the cross-section obtained is a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ which is not a trapezoid. The lines $AB$ and $CD$ meet at point $P$. Determine all values that the distance from point $P$ to the plane of the base of the pyramid can take.
Determine all positive integers that are $11$ times as large as the sum of their digits.

$2n$ players took part in a table tennis tournament. Each player played at most one match against each other player. After the tournament it turned out that exactly $n$ players had played two matches each, and the remaining $n$ players had played three matches each. Determine all positive integers $n$ for which such a situation is possible.
A circle with centre $S$ and a point $D$ lying on this circle are given. A chord $AB$ meets segment $SD$ at point $C$, different from point $S$. Prove that $AB>2CD$.
Positive real numbers $a$, $b$ have the property that the number $$\frac{a-b}{a+b}$$ is rational. Prove that the number $$\frac{2a-b}{2a+b}$$ is also rational.
Is there a convex polyhedron which has an odd number of edges and each of whose faces has an even number of sides? Justify your answer.
Integers $a,b,c>1$ are given such that the greatest common divisor of the numbers $a-1$, $b-1$, $c-1$ is greater than $1$. Prove that the number $abc-1$ is composite.

Finitely many (and more than one) distinct real numbers were written on a board. It turned out that for every two numbers written, their sum was also written. Which numbers were written on the board? Give all possibilities. Justify your answer.

Point $P$ lies inside triangle $ABC$. Points $D$, $E$, $F$ are the points symmetric to point $P$ with respect to the lines $BC$, $CA$, $AB$, respectively. Prove that if triangle $DEF$ is equilateral, then the lines $AD$, $BE$ and $CF$ meet at one point.
Five positive real numbers are given. Prove that two numbers $a$, $b$ can be chosen from among them for which $$0\leqslant \frac{1}{1+a}-\frac{1}{1+b}<\frac{1}{4}.$$
Is there a convex polyhedron with exactly $100$ faces, at least one of which is a 99-gon, such that exactly three edges meet at each of its vertices? Justify your answer.
Are there integers $a$ and $b$ such that the numbers $$a^2+b \quad\text{and}\quad a+b^2$$ are consecutive integers? Justify your answer.
A regular 99-gon is given. Determine the number of isosceles triangles whose vertices coincide with vertices of the given polygon.

Point $I$ is the centre of the circle inscribed in triangle $ABC$. The circle tangent to line $AI$ at point $I$ and passing through point $B$ meets side $BC$ at point $P$ (different from $B$). Lines $IP$ and $AC$ meet at point $Q$. Prove that point $I$ is the midpoint of segment $PQ$.
The numbers $p$ and $q$ are distinct primes. Prove that the number $p^2+q^2$ is not divisible by the number $p+q$.
Points $A_1$, $A_2$, $A_3$, $\ldots$, $A_{100}$ lie inside a disc of radius $1$. Prove that there is a point $P$ on the boundary of this disc for which $$PA_1+PA_2+\ldots+PA_{100}\geqslant 100.$$
Determine all real numbers $x$ for which the numbers $x+\sqrt{3}$ and $x^2+\sqrt{3}$ are rational.

A convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ is given. Points $K$ and $L$ are the midpoints of sides $BC$ and $AD$, respectively. The perpendicular bisectors of segments $AB$ and $CD$ meet segment $KL$ at points $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Prove that if $KP=LQ$, then the lines $AB$ and $CD$ are parallel.
Positive integers $a$, $b$ are given such that the product $ab$ is divisible by the sum $a+b$. Let $d$ be the greatest common divisor of the numbers $a$ and $b$. Prove that $$d\geqslant\sqrt{a+b}.$$
A positive integer $n$ is given. Prove that in the decimal representation of the number $$\sqrt{100^n+2}$$ the digit in the $n$-th place after the decimal point is $0$.
Is it possible, on the surface of every tetrahedron, to find four points which are the vertices of a square and no two of which lie on one face of this tetrahedron? Justify your answer.
Integers $a$, $b$, $c$ satisfy the condition $a+b+c=bc$. Prove that the number $(a+b)(a+c)$ is divisible by $4$.

$99$ people met at a party. It is known that among any three people one can point to one who knows the other two people of this trio. Prove that some person knows all the other people present at the party.

Note. We assume that if person $A$ knows person $B$, then person $B$ knows person $A$.

A triangle $ABC$ is given in which $\angle ACB=120^\circ$. Point $M$ is the midpoint of side $AB$. Points $P$ and $Q$ are chosen on segments $AC$ and $BC$, respectively, such that $AP=PQ=QB$. Prove that $\angle PMQ=90^\circ$.
The numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ are greater than $2$. Prove that at least two of the numbers $$\frac{ab}{c},\quad \frac{bc}{d},\quad \frac{cd}{a},\quad \frac{da}{b}$$ are greater than $2$.
Is there a convex polyhedron which has an odd number of faces and at each of whose vertices an even number of edges meet? Justify your answer.
Five positive real numbers are given such that the product of any two of them is less than the product of the remaining three. Prove that each of the given numbers is greater than $1$.

A triangle $ABC$ is given in which $AC=8$ and $BC=10$. Point $M$ is the midpoint of side $AB$. The circle with centre at point $M$ has radius of length $1$. Prove that there is exactly one point $P$ on this circle for which $\angle APC=90^\circ$.
Positive integers $a$, $b$ have the property that the number $4ab$ is divisible by the number $a^2+b^2$. Prove that $a=b$.
$51$ points were chosen from among the vertices of a regular 100-gon. Prove that among the chosen points there are three which are the vertices of an isosceles right triangle.
Is there a convex polyhedron such that at least four edges meet at each of its vertices and which can be cut by some plane so that the cross-section is a triangle? Justify your answer.
Prove that every integer greater than $5$ can be written as the sum of a prime number and a composite number.

Every positive integer was painted in some colour. It turned out that for every pair of integers $a$, $b$ greater than $1$, the numbers $a+b$ and $ab$ have the same colour. Prove that all numbers greater than $4$ were painted with the same colour.

A convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ is given in which $$\angle DAB+\angle ABC=90^\circ.$$ Point $M$ is the midpoint of side $CD$. Knowing the lengths of segments $AD$ and $BC$, which are equal to $a$ and $b$ respectively, compute the value of the expression $[ABM]-[DAM]-[BCM]$.

Note. The symbol $[\mathcal{F}]$ denotes the area of the figure $\mathcal{F}$.
Positive integers $a$ and $b$ are given such that the numbers $$a^2+2b+1 \quad\text{and}\quad b^2+2a+1$$ are squares of some natural numbers. Prove that $a=b$.
Is there a convex polyhedron exactly one of whose faces is not a regular polygon? Justify your answer.
Positive integers $m$ and $n$ are given such that the number $m+n^2$ is divisible by $m+n$. Prove that the number $m+n^3$ is divisible by $m+n$.
Positive numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ are not greater than $2$. Prove that $$a+b+c+2\geqslant abc.$$

An equilateral triangle $ABC$ is given. Point $P$ lies on the shorter arc $AB$ of the circle circumscribed about this triangle. Point $M$ is the midpoint of segment $AC$. Point $Q$ is symmetric to point $P$ with respect to point $M$. Prove that $BQ=PQ$.
Can a rectangular box of dimensions $8\times 8\times 9$ be assembled from $32$ rectangular blocks of dimensions $2\times 3\times 3$? Justify your answer.
Is there a convex polyhedron in which every edge is a side of some heptagonal face of this polyhedron? Justify your answer.
Positive integers $a$, $b$, $c$ are given for which the number $$\frac{a\sqrt{2}+b}{b\sqrt{2}+c}$$ is rational. Prove that the number $ab+bc+ca$ is divisible by the number $a+b+c$.

Point $D$ lies on side $AB$ of triangle $ABC$. Point $E$ lies on segment $CD$. Prove that if the sum of the areas of triangles $ACE$ and $BDE$ is equal to half the area of triangle $ABC$, then point $D$ is the midpoint of side $AB$ or point $E$ is the midpoint of segment $CD$.

Positive integers $a$ and $b$ are given such that each of the numbers $$ab \quad\text{and}\quad (a+1)(b+1)$$ is the square of an integer. Prove that there is an integer $n>1$ for which the number $(a+n)(b+n)$ is the square of an integer.

In a convex hexagon $ABCDEF$ the interior angles at vertices $B$, $C$, $E$, $F$ are equal. Moreover, the equality $$AB+DE=AF+CD$$ holds. Prove that the line $AD$ and the perpendicular bisectors of segments $BC$ and $EF$ have a common point.

There are $n$ matches on a table, forming $n$ one-element piles. Adam wants to combine them into one $n$-element pile. He will do this using $n-1$ operations, each of which consists of merging two piles into one. Adam agreed with Bartek that every time Adam merges an $a$-element pile with a $b$-element pile, he will receive $a\cdot b$ sweets from Bartek. What is the largest possible number of sweets Adam can receive after performing the $n-1$ operations? Justify your answer.
Positive odd numbers $a$, $b$ have the property that the number $a^b b^a$ is the square of a natural number. Prove that the number $ab$ is the square of a natural number.

A trapezoid $ABCD$ with bases $AB$ and $CD$ is given in which $AB+CD=AD$. The diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ meet at point $E$. The line passing through point $E$ and parallel to the bases of the trapezoid meets the leg $AD$ at point $F$. Prove that $\angle BFC=90^\circ$.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Each of the numbers $1,2,3,\ldots,1000$ was painted with one of $n$ colours. It turned out that every two numbers one of which is a divisor of the other are painted with different colours. Determine the smallest number $n$ for which such a situation is possible.
Real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ are nonzero and satisfy the system of equations $$\begin{cases} a^2+a=b^2\\ b^2+b=c^2\\ c^2+c=a^2. \end{cases}$$ Prove that $(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)=1$.

Point $M$ is the midpoint of side $AB$ of an equilateral triangle $ABC$. Points $D$ and $E$ lie on segments $AC$ and $BC$, respectively, and $\angle DME=60^\circ$. Prove that $AD+BE=DE+\frac{1}{2}AB$.
Integers $a$ and $b$ are greater than $1$. Prove that if one of the numbers $$\frac{a}{b},\quad \frac{a-1}{b-1}$$ is greater than the other by $1$, then both of them are integers.
A trapezoid $ABCD$ with bases $AB$ and $CD$ is given in which $AC=BC$. Point $M$ is the midpoint of the leg $AD$. Prove that $$\angle ACM=\angle CBD.$$

Nonzero real numbers $x$, $y$, $z$ are given for which $x+y+z=0$. Knowing that the numbers $$\frac{x}{y}+\frac{y}{z}+\frac{z}{x} \quad\text{and}\quad \frac{x}{z}+\frac{z}{y}+\frac{y}{x}+1$$ are equal, determine their common value.

Point $D$ lies on side $AB$ of triangle $ABC$. Suppose that there is a point $E$ on segment $CD$ such that $$\angle EAD=\angle AED \quad\text{and}\quad \angle ECB=\angle CEB.$$ Prove that $AC+BC>AB+CE$.

One of the numbers $-1$, $0$ or $1$ was written in each cell of a $5\times 5$ board. It turned out that in every $2\times 2$ square made up of cells of the board, the sum of some three of the four written numbers is equal to zero. What is the largest possible sum of all the numbers written in the cells of the board? Justify your answer.
Positive integers $a$, $b$ and $n$ satisfy the equality $$\frac{a}{b}=\frac{a^2+n^2}{b^2+n^2}.$$ Prove that the number $\sqrt{ab}$ is an integer.
In a right triangle $ABC$, point $M$ is the midpoint of the hypotenuse $AB$. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on segments $AM$ and $MB$, respectively, and $PQ=CQ$. Prove that $AP\leqslant 2\cdot MQ$.

$16$ players took part in a badminton tournament. Each player played at most one match against each other player, and no match ended in a draw. After the tournament it turned out that each of the players had won a different number of matches. Prove that each of the players had lost a different number of matches.

Points $M$ and $N$ lie on side $AB$ of a scalene triangle $ABC$ such that $AN=AC$ and $BM=BC$. The line parallel to $BC$ passing through point $M$ and the line parallel to $AC$ passing through point $N$ meet at point $S$. Prove that $\angle CSM=\angle CSN$.

Natural numbers $a$, $b$ are given which in decimal notation are written with the same digits (that is, each of the digits from $0$ to $9$ occurs the same number of times in the notation of $a$ as in the notation of $b$). Prove that if $a+b=10^{1000}$, then the numbers $a$ and $b$ are divisible by $10$.

A square $ABCD$ with side $1$ is given. Points $K$, $L$, $M$, $N$, different from the vertices of the square, lie on segments $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DA$, respectively. Prove that the perimeter of at least one of the triangles $ANK$, $BKL$, $CLM$, $DMN$ is less than $2$.
Determine all positive integers $n$ for which both numbers $$1\underbrace{77\ldots7}_{n\text{ sevens}} \quad\text{and}\quad 3\underbrace{77\ldots7}_{n\text{ sevens}}$$ are prime.
A parallelogram $ABCD$ is given in which $\angle ABD=90^\circ$ and $\angle CBD=45^\circ$. Point $E$ lies on segment $AD$, and $BC=CE$. Determine the measure of angle $BCE$.
Determine all triples $(a,b,c)$ of nonzero integers for which $$(1-a)(1-b)(1-c)=(1+a)(1+b)(1+c).$$

In the table shown below, Zosia put minus signs in front of eight numbers, changing them into their opposites. It turned out that in every row and in every column there were exactly two negative numbers. Prove that after this change the sum of all sixteen numbers in the table is equal to $0$. $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}\hline 1&2&3&4\\ \hline 5&6&7&8\\ \hline 9&10&11&12\\ \hline 13&14&15&16\\ \hline\end{array}$$
Are there nonzero real numbers $x$, $y$, $z$ such that $$x+\frac{1}{y}=z,\quad y+\frac{1}{z}=x,\quad z+\frac{1}{x}=y?$$ Justify your answer.

Integers $a$ and $b$ are given with $a>b>1$, and the number $b$ is the largest of those divisors of the number $a$ which are different from $a$. Prove that the number $a+b$ is not a power of $2$ with an integer exponent.

A triangle $ABC$ is given in which $AC<BC$ and $\angle ACB=60^\circ$. Point $D$, different from $A$, lies on segment $AC$ with $AB=BD$, and point $E$, different from $B$, lies on line $BC$ with $AB=AE$. Prove that $\angle DEC=30^\circ$.

An odd number $n\geqslant 1$ is given, together with $n$ arrows placed in a row from left to right, each arrow pointing either to the left or to the right. Prove that some arrow is pointed at by exactly as many arrows as it itself points at.

Note: For example, for $n=5$ and the arrangement $\rightarrow\rightarrow\leftarrow\leftarrow\rightarrow$, the successive arrows (from the left) point at $4$, $3$, $2$, $3$, $0$ arrows, respectively.
Determine all pairs of positive integers $m$, $n$ with the property that the $(m+n)$-digit number $$\underbrace{33\ldots3}_{m}\underbrace{66\ldots6}_{n}$$ is the square of an integer.

Decide whether there exists a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ in whose interior one can find a point $P$ satisfying the conditions $$AB=AP,\quad BC=BP,\quad CD=CP,\quad DA=DP.$$

Note: A polygon is called convex if all of its interior angles have measure less than $180^\circ$.

Determine the smallest integer $n\geqslant 1$ with the property that an $n\times n$ square can be cut into square pieces of dimensions $1\times 1$ or $2\times 2$ in such a way that the same number of pieces of each of these two kinds is obtained.

Real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ satisfy the conditions $a+b
eq 0$, $b+c
eq 0$ and $c+a
eq 0$. Prove that $$\left( rac{a^2c}{a+b}+ rac{b^2a}{b+c}+ rac{c^2b}{c+a}ight)\cdot\left( rac{b^2c}{a+b}+ rac{c^2a}{b+c}+ rac{a^2b}{c+a}ight)\geqslant 0.$$

An isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AC=BC$ is given. Points $P$, $Q$, $R$ lie on the sides $AB$, $BC$, $CA$ of this triangle, respectively, and the quadrilateral $CQPR$ is a parallelogram. Prove that the point symmetric to point $P$ with respect to line $QR$ lies on the circle circumscribed about triangle $ABC$.
Let $S=\underbrace{111\ldots1}_{19}\underbrace{999\ldots9}_{19}$. Prove that the $2S$-digit number $$\underbrace{11111\ldots111}_{S}\underbrace{99999\ldots999}_{S}$$ is divisible by $19$.
Is there a tetrahedron whose edge lengths are six distinct integers whose sum is equal to $25$? Justify your answer.

Boys and girls take part in a certain party. Each person taking part in this party knows, among the other people, exactly $3$ boys and exactly $7$ girls. Prove that the number of all people taking part in this party is divisible by $20$.

Note. We assume that if person $A$ knows person $B$, then person $B$ knows person $A$.
Determine all pairs of prime numbers $(p,q)$ for which the number $pq+4$ is the fourth power of a prime number.

A rhombus $ABCD$ is given in which $\angle ABC=100^\circ$. Point $P$ lies on side $CD$, and $\angle PBC=20^\circ$. The line parallel to side $AD$ passing through point $P$ meets the diagonal $AC$ at point $Q$. Prove that $BP=AQ$.

In each cell of a $5\times 5$ board there is an arrow pointing up, down, left or right. Prove that exactly twenty arrows can be removed from this board so that no two of the remaining five arrows point at the same cell.

Note. We assume that each arrow points at all the cells lying in the direction in which it points. No arrow points at the cell in which it is located.

Determine all integers $n\geqslant 1$ with the property that appending an additional digit $1$ on the left of the decimal representation of the number $n^2$ yields the decimal representation of the number $n^3$.
In a certain triangle the measures of the interior angles are $a^\circ$, $b^\circ$, $c^\circ$, where $a^2+b^2=c^2$. Prove that this triangle is acute.

$101$ people took part in a chess tournament. Each pair of participants played exactly one game, which ended in a win for one of them or in a draw. Could it have happened that each participant of this tournament won exactly as many games as they drew? Justify your answer.

A triangle $ABC$ is given. Point $D$ lies on side $BC$, and point $E$ lies inside triangle $ABD$, with $$\angle ABE=\angle CBE \quad\text{and}\quad \angle BAE=\angle EAD=\angle DAC.$$ Prove that if the points $A$, $C$, $D$, $E$ lie on one circle, then triangle $ABC$ is isosceles.

One of the numbers $0$, $1$, $2$, $3$, $4$ was written in each cell of a $21\times 21$ board. If the number $n$ was written in some cell, then the number $n$ was also written in exactly $n$ of the cells adjacent to it. For example, every cell containing the number $2$ is adjacent to exactly two other cells containing the number $2$. Prove that the number of cells in which $0$ was written is odd.

Note. Cells are adjacent if they have exactly one common side.
